content.title: About
content.content: Pearl onions are small, round onions harvested from the onion plant (Allium cepa). After cooking they become tender, mildly sweet and retain a distinctive aroma. They are used in salads, side dishes and as an ingredient in soups.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Pearl onions are a staple in Asian cuisine, especially Korean and Japanese dishes.
Cooking preserves most of their B‑vitamins and vitamin C.
Small onions are digested more easily than larger varieties.
Sulfur compounds in onions become milder and sweeter when boiled.
In some cultures pearl onions are considered a delicacy and served as a snack.

items.title: Rich in antioxidants
items.content: Onions contain quercetin and sulfides that help protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Supports cardiovascular health
items.content: Phytochemicals in onions may lower cholesterol and improve vascular tone.

items.title: Boosts immunity
items.content: Vitamin C and other micronutrients enhance the body’s defense mechanisms.

items.title: Helps regulate blood sugar
items.content: Sulfur compounds can improve insulin sensitivity.

items.title: Aids digestion
items.content: The fiber in pearl onions supports normal bowel function.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to onions, ranging from mild itching to anaphylaxis.

items.title: Gas and bloating
items.content: Onions contain fructans that can cause bloating and discomfort in sensitive digestive systems.

items.title: Medication interactions
items.content: Large amounts of onion may enhance the effects of anticoagulant drugs.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Cooked pearl onions can be added to salads, used as a side dish for meat or fish, incorporated into stews and soups, or served cold as a garnish with a light dressing.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store cooked onions in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. For longer storage, freeze them in portion‑size bags.
